assertion: Earth — Earth's surface supports extensive liquid-water oceans.
Mars — Mars has two small natural satellites named Phobos and Deimos.
Mercury — Mercury follows the innermost orbit of the Solar System's planets.
Venus — A strong greenhouse effect beneath Venus's dense atmosphere keeps its surface intensely hot.
Terrestrial planets — The four inner worlds are terrestrial planets, built mainly from rock and metal.
Saturn — Titan is a moon of Saturn and orbits the planet beyond its main rings.
Jupiter — Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto are the four large Galilean moons of Jupiter.
Uranus — Uranus has an extreme axial tilt, so its poles point roughly along its orbital plane.
Neptune — Neptune's atmosphere contains methane, which absorbs red light and contributes to its blue colour.
Ice giants — Uranus and Neptune contain more volatile ices in their interiors than Jupiter and Saturn.
Phobos — Phobos is the larger of Mars's two small moons and orbits very close to the planet.
Europa — Europa's fractured ice shell is thought to cover a global subsurface ocean.
Titan — Titan is wrapped in a dense atmosphere dominated by nitrogen.
Io — Tidal flexing by Jupiter and neighbouring moons powers Io's intense volcanism.
Triton — Triton's retrograde orbit suggests that Neptune captured it.
Ursa Major — The familiar Big Dipper asterism forms part of Ursa Major.
Orion — Three aligned stars form Orion's Belt near the centre of the constellation.
Cassiopeia — Cassiopeia's five prominent stars form a W or M shape.
Southern Cross — The Southern Cross, formally Crux, is represented by stars on both national flags.
Scorpius — Antares is the prominent reddish star at the centre of Scorpius.
Pupil — The pupil changes size as the iris regulates how much light reaches the retina.
Ears — The ears channel sound vibrations inward, where they are converted into nerve signals.
Smell — Olfactory receptors respond to molecules carried into the nasal cavity.
Taste buds — Taste buds contain receptor cells that respond to substances dissolved in saliva.
Vestibular system — The vestibular system detects head motion and orientation and supports balance.
Skull — The skull surrounds the brain and supports the structures of the face.
Rib cage — The ribs and sternum form a flexible cage around the major chest organs.
Femur — The femur forms the bony core of the thigh and joins the hip to the knee.
Biceps — The biceps brachii contracts to flex the forearm at the elbow.
Achilles tendon — The Achilles tendon transmits force from the calf muscles to the heel.
Mouth — Chewing breaks food apart while saliva moistens it and begins chemical digestion.
Stomach — The stomach mechanically mixes a meal with acidic gastric juice.
Small intestine — The lining of the small intestine provides a large surface for nutrient absorption.
Liver — The liver makes bile, which helps disperse fats in the small intestine.
Large intestine — The large intestine reclaims water from remaining material before waste leaves the body.
Green — In common subtractive pigment mixing, blue and yellow together reflect mainly green light.
Reflection — A mirror forms images because light reflects from its surface.
Prism — A prism refracts different wavelengths by different amounts, separating the colours.
Refraction — Light changes speed and direction when it passes between air and water.
Light scattering — Air molecules scatter shorter visible wavelengths more strongly, making the sky appear blue.
Lever — A seesaw is a rigid bar turning around a central fulcrum, the defining action of a lever.
Pulley — A flagpole pulley changes the direction of the pulling force on the rope.
Wheel and axle — The broad knob acts as a wheel that turns the narrower spindle as an axle.
Inclined plane — An inclined plane reduces the force needed to raise a load by spreading the work over distance.
Screw — A screw thread is a helical inclined plane that converts turning into forward force.
Thermometer — A thermometer responds to temperature and displays a reading.
Wind — Air tends to move from higher-pressure regions toward lower-pressure regions, creating wind.
Fog — Fog consists of tiny water droplets suspended in air near the ground.
Barometer — A barometer measures atmospheric pressure, whose changes often accompany changing weather.
Cumulonimbus — Cumulonimbus clouds grow vertically and can produce heavy rain, lightning, and thunder.
Tropical zone — The tropics receive strong sunlight throughout the year and generally remain warm.
Polar zone — Polar climates are centred on the high-latitude Arctic and Antarctic regions.
Temperate zone — Temperate regions lie between tropical and polar latitudes and often show strong seasonal change.
Arid climate — Arid climates lose more moisture to evaporation than they receive as precipitation.
Mediterranean climate — Mediterranean climates have their dry season in summer and most rain in cooler months.
Granite — Granite is a coarse-grained igneous rock crystallised from slowly cooled magma.
Marble — Metamorphism recrystallises limestone into marble.
Quartz — Quartz is crystalline silicon dioxide and occurs widely in rocks and sand.
Sandstone — Sandstone forms when deposited sand grains are compacted and cemented.
Obsidian — Rapid cooling prevents large crystals from growing, leaving obsidian glassy.
Lava — Molten rock is called magma underground and lava once it erupts onto the surface.
Tectonic plates — Stress builds where tectonic plates interact and is released as earthquakes.
Epicentre — The epicentre lies at the surface above the earthquake focus or hypocentre.
Seismometer — A seismometer detects ground motion; its recording is called a seismogram.
Ring of Fire — Many active plate boundaries around the Pacific create the Ring of Fire.
Mammal — Whales are warm-blooded vertebrates that breathe with lungs and produce milk.
Gills — Water passing across gill surfaces allows oxygen to diffuse into the blood.
Corals — Reef-building coral polyps secrete hard calcium-carbonate skeletons.
Kelp — Large kelps attach to rocky seabeds and create tall, productive underwater habitats.
Plankton — Plankton are organisms unable to swim effectively against the surrounding water movement.
Amazon rainforest — The Amazon rainforest occupies much of the drainage basin of the Amazon River.
Taiga — Taiga forms a broad belt of coniferous forest across high northern latitudes.
Deciduous forest — Deciduous trees drop their leaves during an unfavourable season and grow new ones later.
Mangroves — Mangrove trees tolerate salt and waterlogged sediment along tropical shores.
Canopy — Overlapping branches and leaves form the forest canopy above the understory.
Roots — Roots secure the plant and take up water and dissolved minerals.
Germination — During germination, the embryo resumes growth and emerges from the seed.
Stem — A plant stem supports leaves and contains tissues that move water upward from the roots.
Pollination — Pollination transfers pollen so fertilisation and seed production can follow.
Chlorophyll — Chlorophyll absorbs light for photosynthesis and gives many leaves their green colour.
Six — An adult insect has three pairs of legs attached to its thorax.
Butterfly — Butterflies undergo complete metamorphosis from larva through pupa to winged adult.
Firefly — Fireflies use bioluminescent organs to signal to potential mates.
Queen ant — A colony's queen is the main egg-laying female.
Beetles — Beetles have hardened forewings called elytra covering the hindwings.
Feathers — All living birds have feathers, used for insulation, display, and often flight.
Penguin — Penguins have flipper-like wings adapted for powerful underwater swimming.
Owl — Many owls combine specialised feathers for quiet flight with strong night senses.
Hummingbird — Rapid wing movements let hummingbirds hover while feeding from flowers.
White stork — White storks migrate between European breeding grounds and warmer wintering areas.
Hedgehog — A hedgehog's modified hairs form protective spines, and temperate species often hibernate.
Dolphin — Dolphins breathe air with lungs and therefore surface regularly.
Koala — Koalas are marsupials adapted to a leaf-based diet in Australian eucalyptus forests.
Bats — Bats have forelimbs modified into wings and fly under their own power.
Platypus — The platypus is one of the few living mammals that reproduce by laying eggs.
Frog — During metamorphosis, a tadpole develops legs and lungs and becomes a frog.
Snake — Snakes are elongated reptiles without limbs and with overlapping scales.
Turtle — A turtle's shell is built from bone and fused with parts of its skeleton.
Salamander — Salamanders are amphibians with elongated bodies, tails, and generally moist skin.
Crocodile — Crocodiles are semi-aquatic reptiles whose females lay eggs in land nests.
Tyrannosaurus rex — Tyrannosaurus rex was a large predatory dinosaur whose scientific name means “tyrant lizard king”.
Triceratops — Triceratops is recognised by its horned skull and large bony frill.
Brachiosaurus — Brachiosaurus had longer forelimbs than hind limbs, giving its body an upward slope.
Stegosaurus — Stegosaurus carried distinctive upright plates along its back and spikes on its tail.
Palaeontology — Palaeontologists reconstruct past life and environments from fossils.
Lightning — Lightning is a rapid atmospheric discharge between charged regions.
Copper — Copper combines high electrical conductivity with the ability to be drawn into wire.
Rubber — Rubber resists the movement of electric charge and can act as an insulator.
Battery — Electrochemical reactions inside a battery create a voltage that can drive a flow of electric charge.
Closed circuit — A closed circuit makes a continuous conducting loop between the source and components.
Solid — In ice, water molecules occupy an organised structure that keeps its own shape.
Liquid — Liquid water flows and takes the shape of its container while keeping nearly constant volume.
Gas — Water vapour is gaseous water dispersed among the other gases in air.
Melting — During melting, added energy lets a solid lose its fixed structure and become liquid.
Condensation — Condensation occurs when gas molecules lose enough energy to enter the liquid state.
Nitrogen — Molecular nitrogen accounts for a greater share of dry air by volume than any other gas.
Carbon — Diamond and graphite are allotropes made entirely from carbon atoms arranged differently.
Iron — Iron oxidation in the presence of water produces hydrated iron oxides known as rust.
Helium — Helium is less dense than air and does not burn, making it suitable for balloons.
Sodium — Table salt is sodium chloride, an ionic compound of sodium and chlorine.
Albert Einstein — Einstein reshaped modern physics with special relativity and the geometric theory of gravity.
Isaac Newton — Newton's laws connected motion on Earth with the gravitational motion of celestial bodies.
Marie Curie — Curie's experiments established radioactivity as a major field of physical and chemical research.
Charles Darwin — Darwin presented natural selection as a mechanism by which populations change over generations.
Galileo Galilei — Galileo's telescopic observations of Jupiter's satellites supported a changing view of the cosmos.
Acetic acid — Vinegar is a dilute water solution containing acetic acid.
Baking soda — Sodium bicarbonate reacts with acids to produce bubbles of carbon dioxide.
Oxidation — Rusting is an oxidation process in which iron loses electrons and forms iron oxides.
Acetone — Acetone dissolves many nail-polish ingredients and is widely used in nail-polish removers.
Fermentation — Without oxygen, yeast can metabolise sugars through alcoholic fermentation.
Carbon dioxide — Carbon dioxide dissolves under pressure and escapes as bubbles when the container is opened.
Conduction — Conduction transfers thermal energy through direct contact between materials.
Pectin — Pectin forms a gel under suitable conditions of acidity and sugar, giving jam its set texture.
Caramelisation — Caramelisation creates new colours and flavours as sugar is heated.
Protein denaturation — Heat denatures egg-white proteins, allowing them to form a firm network as the egg cooks.
A shadow — A shadow forms where an opaque object prevents light from reaching a surface.
Thunder — Lightning heats the surrounding air extremely quickly, producing a pressure wave heard as thunder.
Dew — Dew forms when a surface cools below the point at which nearby water vapour condenses.
A mirage — A mirage forms when light bends through layers of air at different temperatures.
A sun dog — A sun dog is a halo phenomenon produced when plate-shaped ice crystals refract sunlight.
The heart — The heart contracts rhythmically to move blood through the circulatory system.
The eardrum — The eardrum transfers sound vibrations from the ear canal to the middle ear.
The iris — Muscles in the iris adjust the pupil and regulate how much light enters the eye.
Insulin — Insulin helps regulate blood glucose by signalling cells to absorb and store it.
The cerebellum — The cerebellum fine-tunes movement and contributes to posture and balance.
Camouflage — Camouflage can hide an animal from predators or help it approach prey.
Hibernation — Hibernation lets some animals survive cold periods when food is scarce.
Seed dispersal — Seed dispersal reduces crowding and helps plants reach new habitats.
Echolocation — Bats emit sounds and analyse the echoes reflected by nearby objects.
Bioluminescence — Bioluminescent organisms create light through chemical reactions in their bodies.
A cell — Cells are the fundamental structural and functional units of living organisms.
A snowflake — The molecular structure of ice leads snow crystals to develop six-sided forms.
A fingerprint — Friction-ridge patterns on fingertips are highly distinctive and persist through life.
Pollen — Pollen grains transfer male genetic material during plant reproduction.
Stomata — Stomata regulate the movement of carbon dioxide, oxygen, and water vapour through a leaf.
Gravity — Earth’s gravity accelerates unsupported objects toward its centre.
Friction — Friction opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact.
Air resistance — A parachute creates a large area that increases aerodynamic drag.
Inertia — Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of motion.
Centripetal force — A centripetal force continually bends an object’s velocity toward the centre of a circular path.
The cheetah — The cheetah’s flexible spine and long limbs support exceptional sprinting speed.
A gecko — A gecko’s toe pads contain tiny hair-like structures that create strong surface contact.
An electric eel — Electric eels generate strong electric discharges with specialised organs in their bodies.
An octopus — An octopus has two branchial hearts for the gills and one systemic heart for the body.
The axolotl — Axolotls can regenerate limbs and repair several other complex tissues.
A volcano — A volcano is an opening or landform through which magma and gases reach the surface.
An earthquake — An earthquake sends seismic waves outward from a rupture in the crust.
An aftershock — Aftershocks occur as the crust adjusts following the initial strong movement in an earthquake sequence.
Subduction — Subduction carries one tectonic plate into the mantle beneath another and can drive earthquakes and volcanism.
A caldera — A caldera forms when the roof above a magma chamber collapses after magma is withdrawn.
balanced forces — Equal, opposite pulls give a net force of zero, so the rope’s motion does not change.
friction — Friction resists motion where surfaces touch and gives tyres their grip.
torque — Torque measures a force’s turning effect; it grows with force and perpendicular distance from the pivot.
buoyancy — Buoyancy is the upward force a fluid exerts on an immersed object.
Magnus effect — The Magnus effect produces a sideways force on a spinning object moving through a fluid such as air.
evaporation — Evaporation is the escape of liquid molecules into a gas from a surface.
boiling point — At the boiling point, vapour bubbles can form throughout a liquid because its vapour pressure matches the surrounding pressure.
deposition — Deposition is the direct transition from a gas to a solid; frost can form this way.
latent heat — Latent heat changes the arrangement of particles during a phase transition instead of raising temperature.
sublimation — Sublimation is a direct change from solid to gas without a liquid stage.
polarization — Polarization describes the orientation of a transverse wave; polarizing filters select particular orientations.
total internal reflection — Total internal reflection occurs when light travelling in the optically denser material meets the boundary above the critical angle.
an afterimage — A negative afterimage appears while the visual system adapts; opponent-colour processing makes the complementary hue stand out.
absorption — Absorption transfers light energy into a material rather than reflecting it.
fluorescence — Fluorescence is prompt visible emission after a substance absorbs higher-energy light.
a nucleotide — Nucleic acids are chains of nucleotides, each built from a sugar, phosphate, and base.
thymine — Two hydrogen bonds join adenine to thymine across the DNA double helix.
messenger RNA — Messenger RNA is transcribed from DNA and presents its sequence to a ribosome for translation.
a codon — The genetic code is read in three-nucleotide units called codons.
CRISPR-Cas9 — CRISPR-Cas9 adapts a bacterial defence mechanism to cut DNA at a sequence selected by guide RNA.
a fever — During a fever, the body raises its temperature set point as part of a coordinated response.
inflammation — Inflammation brings blood flow and immune activity to damaged or infected tissue.
phagocytosis — In phagocytosis, a cell encloses a particle in a membrane-bound compartment and breaks it down.
a T cell — T cells mature in the thymus; helper and cytotoxic types perform different immune roles.
immunological memory — Long-lived memory cells remain after an initial response and react rapidly on later exposure.
an autotroph — Autotrophs form the base of many food systems by producing organic compounds from inorganic material.
decomposers — Decomposers break organic remains into simpler substances that can re-enter nutrient cycles.
a food web — A food web combines intersecting food chains to show who eats whom in a community.
a keystone species — Removing a keystone species can reorganize an ecological community far beyond its numerical share.
ecological succession — During ecological succession, species composition changes over time as organisms alter and recolonize a habitat.
kinetic energy — Kinetic energy depends on mass and the square of speed.
gravitational potential energy — Lifting an object increases its gravitational potential energy, which can become motion as it falls.
conduction — Conduction transfers thermal energy through microscopic interactions without bulk movement of the material.
convection — Convection carries heat through the bulk movement of a liquid or gas.
the law of conservation of energy — Energy conservation requires the total energy of an isolated system to remain constant through transformations.
the mantle — Earth’s mantle is mostly solid rock that can deform slowly over geological time.
a lava tube — A lava tube forms when the crust of a lava flow stays in place after the still-molten interior drains away.
a mid-ocean ridge — Magma rises at divergent boundaries and builds new seafloor along mid-ocean ridges.
continental drift — Continental drift anticipated plate tectonics by arguing that continents had moved and once fitted together.
paleomagnetism — Magnetic minerals can lock in field direction as rock forms, providing evidence for plate movement and field reversals.
humidity — Humidity measures water vapour in air and can be expressed in several ways, including relative humidity.
the dew point — At the dew point, air is saturated with water vapour and further cooling encourages condensation.
a warm front — A warm front commonly brings layered cloud and steadier precipitation as warm air glides over retreating cool air.
the Coriolis effect — In Earth’s rotating reference frame, the Coriolis effect bends large-scale motion rightward in the north and leftward in the south.
the polar vortex — The polar vortex is a broad circulation of low pressure and cold air around a pole, strongest in winter.
a light-year — A light-year measures distance, not time, and is about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
an exoplanet — Exoplanets orbit stars other than the Sun and range from small rocky worlds to gas giants.
redshift — Redshift can result from relative motion, cosmic expansion, or a strong gravitational field.
the transit method — A planetary transit blocks a fraction of starlight, producing a repeatable signature in the light curve.
the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram — The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram reveals groups such as the main sequence, giants, and white dwarfs.
a catalyst — A catalyst provides a reaction pathway with lower activation energy and is regenerated by the end.
the pH scale — The pH scale is logarithmic and relates to hydrogen-ion activity in a solution.
an endothermic reaction — An endothermic reaction takes in thermal energy, so its surroundings may cool.
an emulsion — An emulsion disperses droplets of one immiscible liquid through another, often with an emulsifier for stability.
a buffer solution — A buffer contains components that neutralize modest additions of acid or base, limiting the resulting change in pH.
dormancy — Dormancy prevents a seed from sprouting when conditions are unsuitable for the young plant.
wilting — Water loss reduces turgor pressure in plant cells, leaving leaves and stems limp.
transpiration — This water loss helps pull a continuous stream of water and dissolved minerals upward through a plant.
phototropism — Uneven growth on opposite sides of the shoot curves it toward the light source.
vernalization — Vernalization makes flowering possible after a plant experiences the required low temperatures.
alloys — Combining elements can give an alloy useful properties that its main metal lacks.
vulcanization — Vulcanization creates links between polymer chains, improving rubber’s strength and elasticity.
tempered glass — Controlled heating and rapid cooling place the surface under compression, making the glass stronger and changing how it breaks.
aerogel — In an aerogel, gas replaces most of a gel’s liquid while the delicate solid network remains.
a shape-memory alloy — A reversible change in crystal structure lets this material recover its trained shape as its temperature rises.
classical conditioning — Repeated pairing can make a neutral signal trigger a response that originally followed another stimulus.
Earth’s rotation — The pendulum keeps nearly the same swing direction in space while the ground rotates beneath it.
the double-slit experiment — Waves from the two openings overlap, reinforcing one another in some places and cancelling in others.
the gold foil experiment — The scattering result overturned the diffuse “plum pudding” model and led to the nuclear model of the atom.
the oil-drop experiment — The measured droplet charges came in whole-number multiples of one smallest charge value.
the Moon illusion — The apparent enlargement is a perception effect rather than atmospheric magnification; its exact psychological cause remains unsettled.

assertion: a halo — Hexagonal ice crystals redirect incoming light at characteristic angles, often producing a 22-degree ring.
a fogbow — Fog droplets are much smaller than raindrops, so diffraction smears the colours and leaves a pale or nearly white arc.
a light pillar — Many crystals reflect light toward the observer from slightly different heights, visually joining into a column.
the green flash — Atmospheric refraction and colour separation can make the final visible sliver of the Sun appear green.
a tapeworm — Its flattened body takes up digested nutrients directly from the host’s gut.
a remora — The modified dorsal fin forms a disc that grips a larger marine animal without piercing it.
coral bleaching — A bleached coral is still alive at first, but prolonged loss of its algal partners can lead to starvation and death.
a lichen — The fungal partner provides structure, while the photosynthetic partner supplies organic nutrients.
mycorrhiza — Fungal threads extend the root’s reach through soil, while the plant provides carbon-rich compounds.
huddling — The moving huddle sharply reduces heat loss while continually cycling birds between its exposed edge and warmer centre.
estivation — This reduced-activity state helps an animal survive heat or drought until conditions improve.
torpor — Torpor is a reversible metabolic slowdown that can last for hours and greatly reduce energy use.
diapause — Diapause begins before conditions become severe and ends only after particular environmental cues.
antifreeze proteins — These proteins lower the temperature at which ice crystals can grow in biological fluids.
a Geiger counter — Incoming radiation ionizes gas in the tube, producing an electrical pulse that can be counted.
a calorimeter — Known heat capacities and measured temperature changes allow the exchanged energy to be calculated.
a mass spectrometer — The resulting spectrum shows ion signals at characteristic mass-to-charge values.
a cloud chamber — Ions along a particle’s path act as centres around which tiny droplets form.
an interferometer — A tiny path difference changes the relative phase of the recombined waves and moves the pattern.
the Mohs scale — The scale orders ten reference minerals by scratch resistance rather than measuring hardness in equal numerical steps.
an index fossil — Finding the same diagnostic fossil in separate locations helps geologists correlate the layers.
radiometric dating — A known decay rate turns the measured parent-to-product ratio into a geological clock.
an unconformity — The boundary represents a gap in the local rock record rather than continuous deposition.
uniformitarianism — The principle assumes that the same natural laws and recurring processes can explain geological history.
a synapse — At a chemical synapse, the sending cell releases messenger molecules that bind to receptors on the receiving cell.
a reflex arc — The pathway produces a quick protective response before detailed conscious processing is complete.
myelin — The insulating layers reduce current loss and allow rapid transmission along the fibre.
an action potential — Ion channels open in sequence, producing a self-propagating change in membrane voltage.
saltatory conduction — Regeneration at the nodes of Ranvier makes transmission faster than continuous propagation along every membrane segment.
upwelling — When winds move surface water away, deeper water rises to replace it and carries dissolved nutrients upward.
the thermocline — Within this transition layer, a relatively small increase in depth produces a large temperature drop.
an ocean gyre — Major basins contain rotating current systems that redistribute heat and floating material across great distances.
thermohaline circulation — Cold, salty water sinks in key regions and participates in a connected system of deep and surface flows.
Ekman transport — Friction transfers motion downward while rotational deflection turns successive layers, producing a sideways net flow.
albedo — A high value means a surface returns a large share of incoming energy instead of absorbing it.
a carbon sink — Net uptake stores carbon in biomass, soils, dissolved compounds, or sediments.
ocean acidification — The added carbon dioxide shifts seawater chemistry and reduces the availability of carbonate ions.
a climate proxy — A calibrated relationship lets a preserved natural feature estimate a past climate variable.
Milankovitch cycles — The three orbital variations change seasonal and regional insolation and help pace long-term glacial cycles.
a supernova — This exceptionally energetic event ejects stellar material at high speed and can seed later star systems with heavy elements.
nuclear fusion — When light nuclei combine, a small amount of mass is converted into the energy radiated by a star.
a red giant — The enlarged surface is cooler and therefore redder, while the star’s great size keeps its total luminosity high.
protostar — Gravity heats the contracting object until its central temperature becomes high enough for a stable star to form.
neutron star — Its matter is packed so tightly that a small sample would have an enormous mass under Earth conditions.
superconductivity — The current can persist without the ordinary energy loss caused by electrical resistance.
the photoelectric effect — Electron emission depends on the light’s frequency, which classical wave theory alone could not explain.
wave–particle duality — Neither a purely classical wave nor a purely classical particle model captures every observed result.
the uncertainty principle — The limit is built into quantum mechanics and is not merely a defect of measuring instruments.
quantum tunnelling — A quantum state extends into and sometimes through a classically forbidden region, giving a non-zero crossing probability.
melatonin — Levels normally rise in the evening and fall toward morning as part of the body’s daily timing system.
cortisol — It helps regulate metabolism, immune activity, and the body’s longer-lasting response to demanding conditions.
homeostasis — Living systems continually adjust their activity so vital internal conditions stay within tolerable limits.
negative feedback — The response opposes the original change, preventing the regulated quantity from continually moving in one direction.
the pituitary gland — Its secretions influence growth, reproduction, water balance, and the activity of other glands.
a probiotic — Products sold with this label contain selected living strains rather than simply any fermented ingredient.
the gut microbiome — This living community varies between people and interacts with digestion, metabolism, and immunity.
a biofilm — The surrounding matrix helps the attached cells retain nutrients and withstand environmental stress.
antibiotic resistance — Drug exposure favours resistant survivors, which can reproduce and spread their protective traits.
a bacteriophage — Some reproduce by bursting the infected cell, while others can remain integrated in the host’s DNA.
REM sleep — Brain activity is high during this stage, while most skeletal muscles are temporarily kept from moving.
the amygdala — This paired region helps evaluate threats and link sensory cues with emotionally charged memories.
the corpus callosum — This white-matter bridge lets the hemispheres share sensory, motor, and cognitive information.
hippocampus — This paired structure is crucial for consolidating many new experiences into lasting memory.
Broca’s area — This frontal-language region helps plan and produce spoken language.
event horizon — Crossing this boundary means every possible future path leads farther inward.
dark matter — It does not emit or absorb detectable light, so astronomers infer its presence from gravitational effects.
gravitational lensing — Curved spacetime changes the path of passing light and can magnify otherwise faint background objects.
gravitational waves — Accelerating masses can disturb spacetime, and the disturbance travels outward at the speed of light.
the cosmic microwave background — Expansion stretched this ancient radiation to microwave wavelengths while preserving a snapshot of the young cosmos.
the lateral line — Water movement bends tiny hair cells in canals on or just beneath the skin.
magnetoreception — The ability supplies directional information even when familiar landmarks or stars are unavailable.
electroreception — Specialized receptors around the head respond to tiny voltage differences in the surrounding water.
ultraviolet vision — Their visual receptors are sensitive to wavelengths beyond the human visible range, revealing contrasting paths toward the flower’s centre.
the vomeronasal organ — This chemosensory structure analyzes molecules carried in from the tongue tips.
pH indicators — Their molecular forms absorb different wavelengths as the balance of hydrogen ions changes.
chemiluminescence — Reaction energy raises molecules into excited states, and they release visible light as they return to lower energy.
phosphorescence — The material stores absorbed energy in long-lived excited states, producing an afterglow that can last well beyond illumination.
structural colour — Structures comparable in size to light wavelengths selectively reinforce some reflected colours and suppress others.
chromophore — Changes to this light-absorbing group can shift which wavelengths are removed from white light and therefore alter the observed hue.
brittleness — A brittle solid absorbs relatively little deformation before a crack causes sudden failure.
ductility — Metals with this property can change shape substantially under tension before they fracture.
metal fatigue — Repeated loading can initiate and grow tiny cracks until the remaining section can no longer carry the load.
creep — Sustained stress can produce gradual permanent strain, especially when a material is hot for long periods.
fracture toughness — A higher value means a flawed component can withstand greater stress before rapid crack propagation begins.
stem cell — Its capacity for self-renewal and for producing different descendants makes it valuable in development and tissue repair.
cell differentiation — Selective gene activity guides an initially less specialized cell toward a stable identity and function.
apoptosis — An internal molecular programme packages the cell into fragments that neighbouring cells can safely clear away.
telomere — These protective end regions prevent chromosome tips from fusing with one another or triggering repair responses.
cellular senescence — The lasting growth arrest can block damaged cells from multiplying, although their secretions may affect surrounding tissue.
brackish water — Only species able to tolerate this intermediate and variable salt content thrive across much of the sea.
eutrophication — The surplus nutrients upset the ecosystem by accelerating growth and increasing the amount of organic matter that must decompose.
a cyanobacterial bloom — Buoyant colonies can accumulate at the surface, reducing water quality and sometimes making bathing unsafe.
hypoxia — Severe oxygen shortage can eliminate bottom-dwelling animals and create so-called dead zones.
the halocline — The strong density change across this layer restricts vertical mixing between the upper and lower water masses.
benzene — Its delocalized electrons make all six carbon–carbon bonds equivalent despite the familiar alternating-bond drawing.
structural isomerism — Structural isomers differ in bond connectivity, not merely in how the same connectivity is arranged in space.
chain-growth polymerization — Initiation creates an active centre, propagation lengthens the chain, and termination ends its growth.
chirality — The two nonsuperimposable mirror images are enantiomers and may interact differently with biological molecules.
buckminsterfullerene — Its sixty carbon atoms occupy the vertices of a truncated-icosahedron cage.
half-life — After each such interval, the expected number of undecayed nuclei is halved again.
an alpha particle — Emitting this doubly charged particle lowers the parent nucleus’s atomic number by two and mass number by four.
gamma radiation — This electromagnetic emission often follows another nuclear decay that leaves the daughter nucleus excited.
beta-minus decay — The mass number stays constant, but the new proton raises the atomic number by one.
electron capture — The process lowers the atomic number by one while leaving the mass number unchanged.
genetic drift — Chance alone can make an allele more common, rarer, or lost even when it gives no selective advantage.
the founder effect — The founders carry only a sample of the original gene pool, so rare variants can become unusually common.
a population bottleneck — The survivors represent a restricted genetic sample, and later population growth does not automatically restore lost alleles.
Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium — It provides a null model: departures from its assumptions can reveal evolutionary forces acting on a population.
kin selection — By helping relatives reproduce, an organism can increase the transmission of alleles identical by descent.
an allergy — The triggering substance is an allergen, and symptoms can range from local irritation to a systemic emergency.
an autoimmune disease — Examples include type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, and rheumatoid arthritis, each directed at different self targets.
anaphylaxis — It is a medical emergency commonly treated first with intramuscular epinephrine.
type I hypersensitivity — Allergen binding cross-links IgE on mast cells, prompting rapid release of histamine and other mediators.
molecular mimicry — An immune response raised against the microbe can then recognize a structurally similar self antigen.
the active site — Its three-dimensional shape and chemical groups position the substrate for reaction.
a coenzyme — Such molecules can carry electrons or chemical groups between reactions and are a type of cofactor.
competitive inhibition — The inhibitor reduces substrate binding without lowering the catalytic capacity of enzyme molecules that do bind substrate.
an allosteric site — A regulator binding there can stabilize a more active or less active shape of the enzyme.
a zymogen — Producing the enzyme in an inactive form helps prevent it from acting in the wrong place or at the wrong time.
a nucleosome — Repeating units compact the genome while still allowing regulated access to the DNA.
DNA methylation — The mark can influence protein binding and chromatin state without changing the nucleotide sequence.
histone acetylation — Acetyl groups weaken histone–DNA attraction and create binding sites for proteins that support gene activity.
X-chromosome inactivation — The chromosome is selected early in development, creating a mosaic of cells with different active X chromosomes.
genomic imprinting — Parent-specific marks silence one copy of certain genes, so only the maternal or paternal allele is expressed.
a P wave — This longitudinal wave travels through solids, liquids, and gases faster than other seismic waves.
an S wave — Fluids do not resist the shear deformation this transverse wave requires.
a seismic shadow zone — These gaps in global recordings revealed major boundaries and a liquid layer deep inside Earth.
the moment magnitude scale — It is logarithmic and avoids the saturation problem that limits older magnitude scales for very large earthquakes.
elastic rebound theory — Tectonic motion slowly stores strain until friction is overcome and the fault slips.
a supercell — Strong vertical wind shear lets the storm organize around its rotating updraft.
a mesocyclone — It is much wider than a tornado and can exist without producing one.
the Enhanced Fujita scale — Damage indicators and degrees of damage support an estimated wind-speed range rather than a direct measurement.
a wall cloud — It forms where humid inflow rises into the updraft; rotation increases concern but does not guarantee a tornado.
a hook echo — The shape reveals precipitation curving around rotation, though radar velocity data provide additional evidence.
the Chandra X-ray Observatory — Orbiting above the atmosphere lets it observe radiation that air would otherwise absorb.
an accretion disk — Angular momentum keeps infalling material in orbit while internal stresses move it gradually inward.
a pulsar wind nebula — The particle wind produces synchrotron radiation, with the Crab Nebula as the best-known example.
an X-ray binary — Gas heated while falling toward a neutron star or black hole can become an intense source of energetic photons.
grazing-incidence optics — Nested, nearly cylindrical mirrors guide the rays through one or more shallow reflections to a focus.
countershading — Opposite shading counters the natural pattern of light and shadow on a three-dimensional body.
dermal denticles — Each small structure has enamel-like and dentine-like tissues and points backward with the flow.
the nictitating membrane — The movable membrane shields the exposed eye, including during close contact with prey.
yolk-only viviparity — Unlike matrotrophic modes, the embryo’s entire energy supply comes from yolk deposited before gestation.

assertion: tonic immobility — Researchers use this involuntary response to handle certain sharks, although susceptibility varies among species.
ecdysis — A new soft cuticle forms beneath the old one, then expands and hardens after the old covering splits.
hemolymph — Unlike vertebrate blood, it is not confined entirely to vessels and usually carries little respiratory oxygen in insects.
chelicerae — These appendages serve feeding or defence roles in spiders, scorpions, mites, horseshoe crabs, and their relatives.
book lungs — Gas exchange occurs across the many thin plates, which provide a large surface area inside the abdomen.
Malpighian tubules — They secrete solutes and waste into the tubules while water and useful ions can later be reabsorbed.
the keel — The projecting ridge greatly enlarges the breastbone area available to the main flight muscles.
the furcula — The fused collarbones act as a springy brace between the shoulders during flight.
air sacs — These reservoirs move air through the lungs but are not themselves the main site of gas exchange.
the alula — It forms a slot that helps airflow remain attached to the wing at a high angle of attack.
uncinate processes — The overlapping projections brace the rib cage and provide leverage for muscles that move the sternum.
a sporangium — When mature, this structure releases the spores formed inside it.
an ascus — Meiosis followed by a mitotic division commonly produces eight ascospores within this cell.
a basidium — This spore-bearing cell is characteristic of the group that includes mushrooms, puffballs, and rusts.
a puffball — Pressure on the flexible outer wall forces spore-laden air out through a pore at the top.
an earthstar — The opened rays expose and elevate the round inner sac so impacts can disperse its spores.
marine snow — This sinking material carries surface-produced carbon and nutrients to animals and microbes far below.
chemosynthesis — Chemical reactions replace sunlight as the energy source at the base of these ecosystems.
a whale fall — Its soft tissue, bones, and sulphide-rich decay create several ecological stages on an otherwise food-poor seabed.
a photophore — Reflectors, lenses, filters, or shutters can shape and control the light made within this organ.
counterillumination — By matching the brightness overhead, an animal becomes harder to detect against the lighter surface waters.
polymerase chain reaction — Primers mark the segment’s ends, and a heat-stable polymerase copies it during each cycle.
gel electrophoresis — Smaller fragments usually travel farther through the gel’s network, producing a pattern of bands.
a restriction enzyme — Different members recognise different short sequences and can leave blunt or overhanging ends.
DNA ligase — It forms phosphodiester bonds between adjacent DNA ends, completing the recombinant molecule.
Sanger sequencing — Separating the terminated fragments by length reveals the order of bases in the copied strand.
a nephron — Each unit begins with a renal corpuscle and continues through tubule segments that reabsorb or secrete substances.
the glomerulus — Blood cells and most large proteins stay in the circulation while smaller components enter the surrounding capsule.
Bowman’s capsule — The space between its layers collects the filtrate before it flows into the first tubule segment.
the loop of Henle — Its limbs differ in permeability and transport, creating a countercurrent multiplier in the medulla.
the collecting duct — Hormone-regulated water recovery here is a major determinant of the final urine concentration.
a fumarole — Groundwater heated by magma can emerge through this vent as steam mixed with volcanic gases.
a pyroclastic flow — Its speed, heat, and dense load of debris make it one of the most destructive eruption hazards.
a lahar — Heavy rain, melted snow, or a crater lake can mix with loose eruption material and send this flow far downstream.
pillow lava — A glassy skin forms on contact with water, then splits as more molten rock pushes outward.
a phreatic eruption — Rapid expansion of water into steam drives the explosion, so warning signs can be limited.
the lunar phases — Half the Moon is always sunlit, but its position in orbit changes how much of that half is visible from Earth.
a solar eclipse — Observers inside the Moon’s shadow see the solar disc partly or completely covered.
synchronous rotation — Tidal forces slowed the Moon until its rotation period matched its orbital period.
lunar maria — Early telescope users mistook these smoother, darker impact basins for bodies of water.
earthshine — Earth first reflects sunlight to the Moon, which then reflects a small portion back to the observer.
a succulent — Its enlarged tissues hold water that can support the plant through long dry periods.
the waxy cuticle — Its waxes form a barrier that limits uncontrolled water loss from exposed surfaces.
burrowing — Soil buffers rapid temperature swings and slows the loss of moisture to dry moving air.
nocturnality — Cooler nights reduce heat stress and can also lower the water cost of activity.
CAM photosynthesis — Separating carbon uptake from daytime sugar production limits water loss in hot, dry conditions.
rodents — Gnawing keeps the hard-fronted incisors worn to a useful cutting edge as they continue growing.
cetaceans — Members breathe air through blowholes, nurse their young, and propel themselves with horizontal tail flukes.
monotremes — They produce milk but lack nipples, and they survive naturally only in Australia and New Guinea.
pinnipeds — Their limbs are modified as flippers, yet they still depend on air and return to solid surfaces for key life stages.
the mustelids — This family ranges from aquatic otters to powerful badgers and includes many long-bodied hunters.
frequency — More vibration cycles per second generally produce a higher perceived pitch.
amplitude — A larger value means greater pressure variation and usually greater sound intensity.
an echo — The reflecting surface must be far enough away for the returning sound to be distinguished from the original.
resonance — Energy is transferred especially efficiently when the driving rhythm matches a natural mode of vibration.
the Doppler effect — Relative motion compresses arriving wavefronts during approach and spreads them out during recession.
a sunspot — It is still extremely hot, but the brighter, hotter surface around it makes it appear dark by contrast.
a solar flare — Rapid magnetic-energy release heats plasma and sends radiation across the spectrum toward space.
the solar wind — It consists mainly of protons and electrons carried outward with the Sun’s magnetic field.
a coronal mass ejection — If the expanding cloud reaches Earth, its magnetic field can strongly disturb near-Earth space.
a geomagnetic storm — Strong coupling between the incoming magnetic field and Earth’s magnetosphere drives currents in space and the ground.
a lizard — Many species can release the tail at a built-in weak point; the replacement contains cartilage rather than a copy of every original structure.
a crab — Limb loss at a specialised break point limits damage, while a small replacement limb develops and enlarges during successive moults.
a sea star — Regenerative ability varies among species, but rebuilding arms is widespread in this group of echinoderms.
the zebrafish — This fish can regenerate cardiac muscle after injury, one reason scientists study it as a model for tissue repair.
a planarian — Planarians contain neoblast stem cells that can produce the many specialised cell types needed to replace missing tissues.
ginkgo — Ginkgo biloba has no close living relatives, although its wider lineage was once much more diverse.
a horseshoe crab — Despite its common name, it belongs among chelicerates alongside spiders and scorpions rather than among crustacean crabs.
a nautilus — Unlike its shell-less octopus and squid relatives, it retains a chambered outer shell resembling those of many extinct cephalopods.
the coelacanth — Modern coelacanths are not unchanged ancestors of land vertebrates, but surviving members of an old lobe-finned branch.
the tuatara — It belongs to Rhynchocephalia, a branch separate from its familiar lookalikes and otherwise known only from extinct forms.
a spider — Many species build webs from several kinds of silk, combining strong support threads with sticky capture spirals.
a beaver — Its dams slow flowing water, expand wetland habitat, and give the lodge an underwater entrance.
termites — The mound is an environmental-control structure around the colony, not simply a solid heap in which every chamber lies.
weaverbirds — Males of many species construct elaborate woven nests that females inspect when choosing a mate.
a bowerbird — The male arranges a courtship display called a bower; the female builds the actual nest elsewhere.
salmon — Many species use smell and other cues to home to their natal river before spawning.
the monarch butterfly — No single individual completes the full annual round trip; descendants continue stages of the route.
the humpback whale — Seasonal movement separates productive high-latitude feeding from breeding and calving in warmer seas.
the Arctic tern — Its winding ocean route links Arctic breeding areas with productive southern waters during the opposite season.
the Christmas Island red crab — The synchronized journey can cover roads and settlements as adults move from inland burrows to the coast.
the Venus flytrap — Repeated stimulation closes the trap quickly, helping the plant distinguish moving prey from a stray raindrop.
a pitcher plant — Nectar attracts visitors to the rim, while the smooth inner surface and downward-pointing hairs hinder escape.
a sundew — The leaf can bend around trapped prey, increasing contact with glands that release digestive enzymes.
bladderwort — A pressure difference pulls water and prey through the trapdoor in a rapid capture movement.
butterwort — One set of glands produces sticky mucilage, while another releases enzymes that digest nutrients from the prey.
white blood cells — The group contains several cell types with different roles in innate and adaptive immunity.
platelets — They stick to the damaged surface, activate one another, and support the protein reactions that stabilise a clot.
blood plasma — It is mostly water but also transports salts and many proteins, including antibodies and clotting factors.
fibrin — Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin strands, which cross-link into a tough supporting mesh.
albumin — Made in the liver, it also carries hormones, fatty acids, bilirubin, and many medicines through the bloodstream.
the troposphere — It touches Earth’s surface, and its temperature generally decreases with height.
the stratosphere — Absorption by ozone warms its upper part, so temperature rises with height through much of the layer.
the mesosphere — It lies above the ozone-bearing region and becomes extremely cold near its upper boundary.
the thermosphere — Sparse atoms absorb energetic solar radiation, producing high measured temperatures despite very little heat content.
the exosphere — Particles can travel long distances without collisions, and some escape Earth’s gravity entirely.
rain — Cloud droplets merge until they are heavy enough to fall while temperatures remain above freezing.
drizzle — Its droplets are smaller than those in ordinary showers and can remain closely packed in the air.
hail — Repeated lifting through supercooled droplets adds shells of ice until gravity overcomes the storm’s updraught.
sleet — It forms near the freezing point when falling flakes melt only partly before reaching the surface.
freezing rain — Supercooled drops remain liquid in the air but solidify when they strike a sufficiently cold surface.
a dandelion — The hair-like pappus slows the seed’s fall and lets moving air carry it away from the parent plant.
the coconut palm — The thick husk protects the seed and traps air, making ocean transport possible.
a tumbleweed — A mature above-ground plant part breaks free, and tumbling gradually releases seeds along its route.
mistletoe — Birds eat the fruit or wipe the clinging seeds from their bills, leaving seeds attached to suitable host bark.
the squirting cucumber — Pressure inside the fruit drives an explosive launch that scatters seeds away from the parent.
a stick insect — Its body shape, colour, and slow movement make it difficult for visual predators to separate from vegetation.
the snowshoe hare — Seasonal colour change helps it blend with the ground, while broad hind feet spread its weight on soft snow.
a hoverfly — Resembling a stinging insect can discourage predators even though the fly itself lacks a sting.
a leaf-tailed gecko — Its colour and ragged body edge can imitate leaves, moss, or bark while it rests motionless by day.
the mimic octopus — It selects different displays in response to threats, combining flexible anatomy with rapid colour control.
a petal — Together these structures form the corolla, whose colour, shape, and scent can guide pollinators.
a sepal — The complete ring of these protective parts is called the calyx.
a stamen — Pollen develops in the anther and carries the male reproductive cells.
the stigma — Compatible grains can germinate there and grow a pollen tube down through the style.
the ovary — Ovules within it can become seeds, while surrounding tissue may mature into the fruit wall.
